passage: I'm Sudha, Tanvir's older sister. Tanvir used to read everywhere: in the bathroom, at dinner, under the blanket with a torch. Then in July his school started a reading chart. Every book finished got a gold star, and ten stars meant a prize. At first he was thrilled. By August I noticed he'd stopped reading the fat adventure book about the ship. He was racing through thin picture books meant for little kids, three a night, and counting his stars before bed. Last Sunday I asked if he wanted to finish the ship book. He said, "It's too long. It's only one star." I can't say what he feels inside. But he doesn't read under the blanket anymore.

qa.q: What did ten stars on the reading chart mean?
qa.a: Ten stars meant a prize.

qa.q: Why might Tanvir call the ship book 'only one star'?
qa.a: He now seems to judge books by how fast they earn stars, so a long book may feel like a frustrating bad deal instead of an adventure.

qa.q: What choice could Tanvir's family make to bring back the old reading?
qa.a: They could read the ship book aloud with him at bedtime with no stars attached, and let him pick books just for fun again.

qa.q: What is it like for Sudha to watch the change?
qa.a: Sudha misses the brother who read under the blanket and feels uneasy seeing stars matter more than stories 😔.

grounding: An older sister watches her brother's love of reading shrink to chasing stars with thin books.

passage:
April: Vasudha spent Saturday afternoon in the library corner, lost in a thick book of folk tales, and borrowed two more before Parul Ma'am closed up.
June: The library announced a summer contest: a bookmark for every book read, and a big prize for the most books. Vasudha picked up five thin comics and asked Parul Ma'am, "Do these count?" She read them in an hour, collected five bookmarks, and grinned.
August: The folk-tale book sat on the returns trolley, untouched. Vasudha was counting bookmarks on her bed: fourteen. When Parul Ma'am asked if she'd liked any story especially, Vasudha thought, then shrugged. "I don't remember. They were short."

qa.q: How many bookmarks did Vasudha have in August?
qa.a: Fourteen bookmarks, counted on her bed.

qa.q: Why did Vasudha grin after reading five thin comics in an hour?
qa.a: She felt pleased to win five bookmarks quickly; the count had started to matter more than the stories.

qa.q: What turning point could Parul Ma'am use to rekindle Vasudha's interest?
qa.a: When Vasudha shrugged 'I don't remember', Parul Ma'am could offer the folk-tale book again and invite her to share one favourite story, no bookmark needed.

qa.q: How might Parul Ma'am feel seeing the folk-tale book untouched?
qa.a: Parul Ma'am may feel sad, having seen Vasudha lost in folk tales in April, and worry the contest pushed that joy aside.

grounding: Over a summer, a girl who loved folk tales switches to thin books for bookmarks and loses the joy.

passage: Siddharth, you want money for each book you read? Let me tell you what happened to your Pradeep dadu. When I was nine, I loved books so much that my mother had to pull them out of my hands at dinner. Then my uncle, meaning well, said he'd give me four annas for every book I finished. Oh, I was rich within a month! But I stopped choosing the thick adventure books with maps. I chose the thinnest ones in the school cupboard, the ones for small children. I finished them on the bus. I couldn't tell you a single story from them. One day I realised I hadn't opened my favourite pirate book in weeks. I asked my uncle to stop the annas. It took me a whole summer to love reading again.

qa.q: What did Pradeep's uncle promise for every book finished?
qa.a: Four annas for every book he finished.

qa.q: Why did Pradeep start choosing the thinnest books?
qa.a: Pradeep felt excited about getting rich, so thin books meant more annas faster, and the coins mattered more than the stories.

qa.q: What choice did Pradeep make when he noticed the change?
qa.a: He asked his uncle to stop the annas, giving himself a chance to read for the story again.

qa.q: How might Siddharth feel about money per book after hearing this?
qa.a: Siddharth might think twice, seeing that Dadu's love of reading faded once coins came in 🤔.

grounding: A grandfather recalls how being paid per book turned him toward thin books until the joy faded.

passage:
Vandana used to disappear into fat books; the one about a girl sailing the Sundarbans took her a whole happy week. Then, in May, Madhuri Masi pinned up a chart: ten rupees for every book finished before school reopened.
With three weeks of holidays left, Vandana started choosing differently. At the library she ran her finger along the spines and pulled out the thinnest ones: picture books for little kids, a twenty-page one about buses. Eleven books in ten days. Eleven stars.
The fat Sundarbans sequel sat on her bed, bookmark still on page three.
'Aren't you reading that one?' Masi asked.
'It's too long. It only counts as one.' Vandana counted her coins and didn't look at the book.

qa.q: How much did Madhuri Masi offer for each finished book?
qa.a: Ten rupees for every book finished before school reopened.

qa.q: Why does the Sundarbans sequel now feel 'too long' to Vandana?
qa.a: Vandana is now thinking about the reward, and a long book 'only counts as one', so the joy of getting lost in a story is pushed aside by counting stars and coins.

qa.q: What choice could Madhuri Masi make now, and why?
qa.a: Masi could quietly drop the per-book payment and ask Vandana about the story she is reading instead; talk about books brings back interest, while the coins keep pointing to thin ones.

qa.q: How might Madhuri Masi feel seeing eleven stars but the sequel untouched?
qa.a: Masi may feel uneasy, realising the chart meant as encouragement has turned reading into a race for coins.

grounding: A child who loved long books is paid per book and starts choosing only thin ones, as the reward crowds out the joy.

passage:
In Class 5 at Bidisha's school in Chennai, Lakshmi Miss started a Reading Badge board: a gold star for every book, a badge for every ten. Bidisha, who used to read under the desk during maths, was the first to reach twenty stars.
But on Sunday in their Adyar flat, her father found her flipping through a slim book in four minutes, then writing its title in her log.
'Didn't you love the detective series?' he asked. 'The one with the missing cat?'
'Those are three hundred pages, Appa. That's a week for one star.'
She pulled out the next thin book. She didn't laugh at anything in it. When she finished, she didn't sit hugging it the way she used to. She just wrote down the title and counted in her head: twenty-one.

qa.q: What did Lakshmi Miss give for every ten books?
qa.a: A badge.

qa.q: What has changed in how Bidisha feels while reading, and what shows it?
qa.a: Bidisha seems bored and flat now: she no longer laughs or sits hugging the book, and just writes the title while counting her stars.

qa.q: What choice could Appa or Lakshmi Miss make to bring back the joy?
qa.a: They could stop counting books and ask Bidisha what happens in the detective series; talking about stories turns attention back to reading itself rather than the star total.

qa.q: How might Lakshmi Miss feel if she saw Bidisha's four-minute flip-through?
qa.a: Lakshmi Miss would likely be disappointed, having meant the board to encourage reading, and might see it was rewarding speed rather than love of books.

grounding: A child who loved reading chases stars for each book and swaps long stories for thin ones, and the joy fades.

passage:
School library note, Class 4, end of term.
Before the reading challenge, Divyansh was the child I had to chase out at the bell. He once spent three weeks on a thick book about volcanoes and told me every chapter. Since we started giving a star sticker for each book finished, with a prize at twenty stars, he has read twenty-two books in six weeks. Almost all are the thin picture books from the lower shelf, which he finishes in ten minutes at the counter. When I asked about the volcano series, he said, 'Those take too long. I'd only get one star.' He no longer tells me what the books are about. He asks how many stars he has. Next step: I'll end the star chart after this month, set up a 'tell me one thing you found' corner instead, and talk to his class teacher.
Afreen

qa.q: How many books has Divyansh read in six weeks?
qa.a: He has read twenty-two books in six weeks.

qa.q: Why does Divyansh now choose the thin picture books?
qa.a: He has become eager for stars and the prize, so the thick books he used to love feel like a waste of time, and his interest in what's inside has faded.

qa.q: What change does the librarian plan, and why?
qa.a: Ending the star chart and starting a 'tell me one thing you found' corner, to bring the focus back to the joy of reading rather than counting.

qa.q: What might Afreen feel noticing he only asks about stars?
qa.a: Afreen likely feels disappointed and a little worried, missing the reader who used to tell every chapter about volcanoes.

grounding: A librarian's note shows a child who loved thick books switching to thin ones once a star reward is offered, as the joy of reading fades.

passage:
Sunday
Papa's new rule: one cricket card for every book I finish. I've got nine cards this week! Yogesh only has four. I picked all the short books from the shelf, the ones with big letters. I finished three today before lunch.
The jungle story book Nani gave me is still on my table. I was really liking it, the part with the wolves. But it's so thick, it would take a whole week, and that's only one card. So I put it back in the cupboard.
Tonight I tried to remember what the short books were about. I couldn't really. One had a dog in it, I think. I just remember the cards.
Chinmay

qa.q: How many cards has Chinmay got this week?
qa.a: Chinmay has got nine cards this week.

qa.q: Why did Chinmay put the thick book back in the cupboard?
qa.a: Chinmay got excited about collecting cards and beating Yogesh, so a slow book worth only one card felt not worth it, even though Chinmay had been enjoying it.

qa.q: What could Papa change to bring back the joy of reading?
qa.a: Papa could stop the card-per-book rule and instead ask Chinmay to talk about favourite parts, like the wolves.

qa.q: How might Nani feel seeing her book back in the cupboard?
qa.a: Nani might feel a little sad, having chosen a book she hoped Chinmay would love.

grounding: A child who enjoyed a thick book abandons it for short ones once a card is offered per book, and forgets what the short books said.

passage: The small library in the panchayat office at Khandala had one shelf of children's books, and Dhruv had read most of them twice, sitting on the floor with his knees up. In June, the volunteer, Zainab Didi, started a scheme: a peda from the sweet shop for every book returned. Dhruv began taking the thinnest books, the ones with twelve pages, and bringing them back the same afternoon. He collected eleven pedas in a week. One day Zainab Didi held up the fat book about sailors he used to love. 'Don't you want this again?' Dhruv shook his head. 'It's just one peda.' He took two thin books instead and ran off without opening either. Zainab Didi watched him go, then quietly took the peda jar off the counter.

qa.q: What did Zainab Didi give for each book returned?
qa.a: She gave a peda from the sweet shop.

qa.q: Why did Dhruv refuse the book about sailors?
qa.a: He had become eager for pedas, so a long book he once loved felt like a poor trade, and his joy in reading slipped behind the reward.

qa.q: What could Zainab Didi do next?
qa.a: Remove the peda scheme, as she begins to, and invite children to share what they liked in a book instead.

qa.q: What might Zainab Didi feel watching Dhruv run off?
qa.a: She likely feels disappointed and a little regretful that her reward scheme changed how he reads.

grounding: A village child who loved reading starts picking the thinnest books once sweets are offered per book, and the joy fades.

passage:
Alejandro used to read long adventure books about ships and castles, under the blanket with a torch, in their flat in Seville.
Then the library started a summer challenge: one sticker for every book finished, and a prize for twenty stickers.
By the second week Alejandro was racing. He chose thin books with big letters. Picture books meant for his little sister Rosa. Four in one afternoon.
“You didn't finish the pirate one,” Rosa said, pointing at the thick book on the shelf.
“It takes too long. It's only one sticker.”
He got his twenty stickers and a shiny medal. At home, he put it on the shelf and sat on the bed. He didn't feel like reading anything. The torch stayed in the drawer.

qa.q: What did the library give for every book finished?
qa.a: One sticker for every book, and a prize for twenty stickers.

qa.q: Why did the pirate book suddenly seem not worth it to Alejandro?
qa.a: He was excited about collecting stickers and impatient with long books that earned only one, so the reward felt more important than the story.

qa.q: What could the library or his family try instead?
qa.a: Reward time spent reading or talk about favourite stories, so the pleasure of the book stays the main thing.

qa.q: How might Rosa see her brother's new reading?
qa.a: Rosa may be puzzled to see him reading her picture books instead of his pirate stories.

grounding: The passage shows a child who loved reading choosing thin books for stickers, and his joy in reading fading as the reward took over.

passage:
The school library had a new chart: “Read and Win!” Each book returned earned one point, and ten points meant a free canteen coupon.
Deepak had always been the boy who read the whole science encyclopedia. Now he stood at the counter with five thin comics.
His friend Samir raised an eyebrow. “You finished the space book?”
“No. Too many pages. Comics are faster.”
By the end of the month Deepak had thirty points and three coupons. But when the librarian put a new book on black holes on the display, the one he would once have grabbed first, he walked past it.
“Aren't you taking that?” Samir asked.
Deepak shrugged. “It's only one point.”
Later, he felt a strange, flat feeling he couldn't name.

qa.q: What did ten points earn in the library challenge?
qa.a: Ten points earned a free canteen coupon.

qa.q: Why did Deepak walk past the new book on black holes?
qa.a: He was focused on points, and a long book was worth only one, so the prize crowded out his old interest and left him feeling flat.

qa.q: What could the librarian change to protect children's interest?
qa.a: Give points for time spent or for sharing what they learned, so long, interesting books aren't punished.

qa.q: How might Samir feel watching his friend walk past the space book?
qa.a: Samir might feel surprised and a little sad, remembering how much Deepak used to love such books.

grounding: The passage shows a child who loved reading switching to thin books for points and losing interest in the kind of books he once enjoyed.

passage:
Before: In June, Pema spent every evening in the window seat with a fat book about a girl who sails around the world. She read slowly, sometimes reading a good page twice.
During: In July, Gargi Masi said, “I'll give you twenty rupees for every book you finish.” Pema's eyes went wide. Next day she took six thin books from the school library. She finished them all by Sunday. The sailing book stayed with its bookmark on chapter nine.
After: By late August, Pema had a tin full of coins. One rainy evening Masi asked, “Why not read your sailing book?” Pema shrugged. “It's so long. And I don't really feel like reading.”
She sat by the window, the tin in her lap, watching the rain.

qa.q: On which chapter was the bookmark in the sailing book?
qa.a: The bookmark stayed on chapter nine.

qa.q: How did Pema feel about reading by late August?
qa.a: She seemed bored and flat about reading; the coins had become the point, and the old joy had faded.

qa.q: What could Gargi Masi try now to bring back Pema's love of reading?
qa.a: Stop paying per book and instead read the sailing book with Pema, talking about the story, so interest leads again.

qa.q: What might Gargi Masi realise when Pema says she doesn't feel like reading?
qa.a: Masi might feel sorry and surprised, realising the reward she meant kindly pushed out Pema's own interest.

grounding: The three beats show a child who loved reading being paid per book, choosing thin ones, and losing her original joy.

passage: Divyansh, you want a rupee for each book? Let your Varun Chacha tell you what happened to me. The summer I was nine, my uncle said, "One rupee for every book you finish." I loved fat adventure books. But with the rupee, something changed. I started counting. A fat book took a week and got one rupee. A thin book took an hour and also got one rupee. So I read thin books. Fifteen in a week! I got fifteen rupees and felt rich. But I stopped enjoying the stories. I skipped pages. By the end of the summer, I didn't want to read at all. My uncle stopped the rupees. It took me months to pick up a fat book again, just because I wanted to.

qa.q: How much did young Varun get for each book?
qa.a: One rupee for every book.

qa.q: Why did young Varun stop enjoying reading?
qa.a: Counting rupees took over the joy, so young Varun felt pressure to finish fast and chose thin books he didn't care about.

qa.q: What turning point in the story brought back Varun's joy in reading?
qa.a: When the uncle stopped the rupees, Varun slowly started reading fat books again just because he wanted to.

qa.q: How might Varun's uncle have felt seeing him stop reading?
qa.a: The uncle was probably puzzled and disappointed, since the reward was meant to help.

grounding: An uncle recalls a childhood summer when a rupee per book made him choose thin books until the joy of reading faded.

passage: The library was closing early for Christmas, and Kishore had fifteen minutes to choose books for the reading challenge. Every book finished earned a gold star on the class chart. Before the challenge, Kishore had loved the thick dinosaur encyclopaedia. Now he grabbed five thin picture books. "Stars," he whispered. Mrs Elizabeth, the librarian, raised her eyebrows. "No dinosaurs this time?" "It's too long. It's only one star." By the end of the holidays Kishore had twenty stars, the most in the class. But when Mrs Elizabeth asked what his favourite book was, he couldn't remember any of them. He stared at the chart. "I don't think I liked reading them," he said slowly. She smiled. "Want to borrow the dinosaur book? No star. Just for you." He hesitated, then nodded.

qa.q: How many gold stars did Kishore get by the end of the holidays?
qa.a: Twenty stars, the most in the class.

qa.q: Why couldn't Kishore remember any of the books?
qa.a: He was chasing stars, so he felt no real interest in the thin books and read them only to count them.

qa.q: What did Mrs Elizabeth do that could bring back Kishore's interest?
qa.a: She offered the dinosaur book with no star, just for him, so he could read for joy again.

qa.q: How might Mrs Elizabeth have felt watching Kishore pick thin books?
qa.a: She was probably a little worried, seeing a boy who loved dinosaurs choose books only for the stars.

grounding: Rushed by the library closing, a boy picks thin books for gold stars and loses the joy of reading he once had.

passage: In the Diwali holidays, Papa offered ten rupees for every book Yogesh finished. Yogesh used to spend whole afternoons with his thick mystery book. Now he went to the library and came back with a pile of thin storybooks. His brother Anand said, "What about your mystery book?" "Too long. Only ten rupees." By the end of the week, Yogesh had finished twelve books and earned a hundred and twenty rupees. But at dinner, when Papa asked which story he liked best, Yogesh couldn't answer. He shrugged. "They were all okay." Anand said, "You used to talk about your books all through dinner." Yogesh went quiet. That night, Papa said, "No more money for books. Read what you like." The next afternoon, Yogesh was back with his mystery book.

qa.q: How much did Papa offer for every book?
qa.a: Ten rupees for every book Yogesh finished.

qa.q: Why couldn't Yogesh name a favourite story that week?
qa.a: He was reading for money, not interest, so he felt nothing for the thin books and they all seemed just okay.

qa.q: Which choice brought back Yogesh's joy, and why?
qa.a: Papa stopping the money, because it let Yogesh read what he loved again for its own sake.

qa.q: How might Anand have seen the change in his brother?
qa.a: Anand noticed and seemed a little sad that Yogesh no longer talked about his books at dinner.

grounding: During Diwali holidays a boy offered money per book reads only thin ones, and his love of reading fades until the reward stops.

passage:
"Mumma, done! That's book number nine. Nine stars!"
"Nine already, Irawati? The summer holidays only started two weeks ago."
"Two more stars and I get the art set."
"And the big one Nani sent, about the girl who sails to the islands? You were so excited about it."
"That one's too thick. It would take a week. That's only one star for a whole week."
"But you loved the first chapter. You read it under the blanket with a torch."
"...Yeah. But the thin ones are faster, Mumma."
"Hmm. What if we forget about stars for the sailing book?"
"Then why would I read it?"
Alka put down her tea and looked at her daughter for a long moment.

qa.q: What does Irawati get after two more stars?
qa.a: The art set.

qa.q: Why does Irawati now skip the thick sailing book?
qa.a: Irawati is eager for stars, and a thick book earns only one star in a week, so the prize now matters more than the story she once felt excited about.

qa.q: What could Alka try to bring back the joy of reading?
qa.a: Drop the stars for reading, talk together about the stories, and let Irawati pick up the sailing book just for fun, maybe reading the next chapter together.

qa.q: What might Alka be feeling when Irawati asks "Then why would I read it?"
qa.a: Alka seems worried and a little sad, realising the reward has pushed out the love of reading she once saw under the blanket.

grounding: A child who loved reading is given a star for each book and starts choosing only thin ones, as the reward pushes out the joy.
